findings.text: These fragments specify guest visible contracts for transport, queuing and timekeeping plus the integer widths they use. The PCI portion covers configuration windows and administration messaging, the ring portion covers descriptor memory and notification control, and the clock portion covers request, response and alarm notification envelopes. No callable routines, locking primitives or driver lifecycle helpers appear here. Consumers interact by reading and writing the described windows and exchanging the described messages.

Device operation and queue operation share one window with distinct access rules. Device wide state handles feature negotiation in two selector plus value pairs, messaging configuration, queue count, operational status and a generation marker that changes when configuration changes. Queue specific state is indirect. One selector chooses the target queue and the following controls apply to it, namely size, messaging vector, enable state, notification offset and three guest addresses for descriptor, available and used areas each conveyed as low plus high halves. Feature values, queue count, generation and notification offset are observed only, while selectors, guest acknowledgement, status, queue choice and the programming controls are written by the driver. Size must be a power of two. Examples include device_status for liveness, config_generation for change detection, queue_select for targeting and queue_enable for activation.

The modern variant preserves the whole common layout and appends queue and administration extensions. It adds a notification payload control and a reset control for the selected queue, plus two read only identities describing the administration queue index and population. A separate small capability pairs a generic PCI capability header with a four byte data area used to reach device registers through BAR access. The appended controls are queue_notify_data and queue_reset, while discovery uses admin_queue_index with admin_queue_num and data movement uses pci_cfg_data.

Capability discovery uses fixed byte positions inside the vendor capability header. The vendor identifier lives at 0 and the link to the next capability at 1, with header length at 2 and configuration type at 3. The BAR selector lives at 4, the offset inside that BAR at 8 and the length at 12. Notification location scaling uses a multiplier of 16.

Device wide fields use fixed byte positions inside the common configuration area. Device feature selection is at 0 with its value at 4, guest feature selection at 8 with its value at 12. Messaging configuration is at 16, queue count at 18, operational status at 20 and configuration generation at 21.

Queue specific fields use fixed byte positions after the device wide area. Queue selection is at 22, size at 24, messaging vector at 26, enable at 28 and notification offset at 30. Descriptor address halves are at 32 and 36, available halves at 40 and 44, used halves at 48 and 52. Notification payload is at 56, reset at 58, administration index at 60 and administration count at 62.

Basic administration uses small numeric codes. Success status is 0. Command list discovery uses 0 for query and 1 for use. Group addressing uses 0 for self and 1 for single root sharing. Legacy transport tunnelling uses 2 for common configuration write, 3 for common configuration read, 4 for device configuration write, 5 for device configuration read and 6 for notification information.

Extended administration opcodes continue the numeric space. Capability identifier list query is 7, device capability fetch is 8 and driver capability publish is 9. Resource object creation is 10 and destruction is 13. Device parts metadata fetch is 14, parts fetch 15, parts update 16 and device mode update 17.

Every administration exchange starts with a routing header carrying an operation code, a group selector, reserved space for future growth and a 64 bit member identifier, and completes with a compact outcome carrying a status code plus qualifier and reserved space. Legacy register tunnelling carries a start offset. The write form adds reserved space plus a flexible register payload while the read form carries only the offset. Notification discovery returns up to four entries, each describing ownership flags, BAR identity, padding and a 64 bit offset, where zero marks termination.

Capability and partitioning management uses paired request and result shapes with flexible tails. Identifier discovery returns a bitmap sized to cover the defined capability set. Single capability fetch and publish share an identifier plus reserved area, with publish adding a variable tail. Resource creation pairs a type header and unique identifier with flags and a variable tail. Partition descriptors combine a type, flags and length with a selector that is either a configuration offset or a queue index, followed by a variable value. Metadata results are a choice among total size, header count, or header count plus headers. Fetch and update payloads reuse the resource header and then carry either a header list or full partitions, while mode update carries only flags.

Administration flags and limits use small values. Notification ownership uses 0 for end, 1 for owner device and 2 for member memory, with at most four entries. The parts capability identifier is 0. Resource type for parts is 0 with get operation 0 and set operation 1. Metadata interrogation uses 0 for size, 1 for count and 2 for list. Optional partition marking is 0, parts fetch uses 0 for selected and 1 for all, and stopped mode uses 0.

Split rings separate description, publication and completion. Each descriptor conveys a guest address, length, control flags and a link to the next element in a chain. The available side publishes driver intent through flags, a moving index and a flexible ring of descriptor heads. Completion is reported as pairs of chain head identifier plus bytes written, grouped under flags and a moving device index with a flexible ring. A host side view aggregates the element count with pointers to the three areas for convenient access.

Split ring control uses single bit flags and small feature numbers plus alignment rules. Chaining uses value 1, device write permission uses 2 and indirect tables use 4. Suppression of device signals and driver interrupts each use value 1 in their respective flag words. Indirect descriptor support is feature 28 and event index support is 29. Required alignments are 2 for available, 4 for used and 16 for descriptors.

Packed rings use dense entries with explicit availability tracking. Each entry carries an address, length, buffer identifier and flags where bit 7 marks availability to the device and bit 15 marks use by the device. A separate event structure carries an offset plus wrap marker and control flags. Event control distinguishes enable at 0, disable at 1 and descriptor selection at 2, with wrap tracking at bit 15.

Clock feature and messaging use partitioned numeric ranges. Alarm support is feature 0. Fast reads use 1 for plain read and 2 for cross read, corresponding to hex 0001 and 0002. Management uses 4096 for configuration, then 4097, 4098, 4099, 4100 and 4101 for clock capability, cross capability, alarm read, alarm set and alarm enable, corresponding to hex 1000 through 1005. Alarm notifications use 8192, hex 2000. Outcome codes are 0 for success, 2 for unsupported, 3 for missing device, 4 for invalid argument and 5 for input output failure.

Clock exchanges share narrow headers and per operation bodies. Request and notification headers carry a message type plus reserved space, while responses carry a status plus reserved space. Plain read passes a clock identifier and returns a 64 bit reading. Cross read adds a hardware counter selector and returns both a clock reading and a counter value. Configuration fetch returns a population count that bounds valid identifiers. Clock capability returns type, smearing behaviour and flags, while cross capability returns flags indicating support.

Alarm handling separates inspection, programming and asynchronous delivery. Inspection passes a clock identifier and returns time plus flags. Programming passes time, clock and flags with no result parameters, and a separate enable control toggles delivery per clock. The request queue and response queue are each a choice among the eight read, cross, configuration, capability and alarm shapes, selected by message type. Alarm delivery carries a clock identifier in a notification, wrapped in a single member queue union.

Clock identity and counter identity use compact enumerations. Virtual count is 0, timestamp counter is 1 and invalid marker is 255, hex FF. Clock types are 0 for UTC, 1 for TAI, 2 for monotonic, 3 for smeared UTC and 4 for possibly smeared UTC. Smearing modes are 0 for unspecified, 1 for noon linear and 2 for stepped UTC slewing. Capability and state use low bit flags for alarm support, cross support and alarm enable.

Cross header integer widths are distinct bitwise types so misuse across endianness domains is detectable, with 16, 32 and 64 bit variants. Each header is protected against multiple inclusion by its own guard macro, making repeated inclusion idempotent.

Feature and queue programming follow select then access discipline. A selector chooses which feature word or queue subsequent reads and writes affect, so drivers must set device_feature_select before sampling device_feature and guest_feature_select before acknowledging through guest_feature, and must set queue_select before touching size, vector, enable, offsets or addresses. Addresses become meaningful only after both halves are written, and enable must follow address and size programming. Status changes bracket initialization, and generation must be rechecked around device configuration reads. Reserved areas stay zero for forward compatibility.

Administration, queuing and clock exchanges share envelope discipline. The routing header determines interpretation of the trailing bytes, and the outcome header must be checked before trusting any result payload. Flexible tails mean message length depends on operation. Receivers must bound register blobs, capability data, header lists and ring entries by negotiated sizes rather than assuming fixed length. Descriptor chains terminate only when the chaining flag is clear, direction is fixed by the write flag, and indirect tables expand in place of a single entry. Available and used indices advance monotonically with wrap, and packed entries toggle availability and use markers with wrap tracking. Clock identifiers are valid only below the reported population, cross reads require prior capability affirmation, and alarm operations require alarm support.

Bring up proceeds from discovery through negotiation to queue activation, with administration and clock use layered on top. After locating capabilities, the driver selects and reads device features, publishes guest features, then per queue selects an index, establishes size, addresses and vector, and finally enables. Notification offset and payload coordinate doorbells, while reset returns a queue to unprogrammed state. Administration advances from list query to capability query, resource creation, metadata sizing and listing, selective or full fetch, update, and mode transition. Clock use advances from configuration to per clock and cross capability checks, then reads or alarm programming with enable gating delivery.

Several shapes invite misuse if handled naively. Split low plus high programming can tear if observed mid update, and stale reads can occur if generation is not rechecked. A non power of two size, an out of range selector, or enabling before addresses are established leaves behaviour undefined here. Flexible rings, register blobs, capability tails and header lists have no self describing length in these fragments, so overrun is possible without external bounds. Unions require out of band knowledge of the active member, and zero valued terminators or flags can be confused with valid data if list handling is careless. Suppressed notifications and disabled events can stall progress if neither side polls, and cross or alarm actions without capability checks can produce unsupported outcomes.
